ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

elbow imaging — clinical pattern 1

An adult has elbow pain after a fall. No fracture line is clearly visible on initial films, but a posterior fat pad is visible on the true lateral radiograph. Joint alignment is maintained. What interpretation should guide further assessment rather than declaring the film normal?

  1. Radial head dislocation
  2. Extension-type supracondylar humerus fracture
  3. Normal radiographic elbow alignment
  4. Olecranon fracture
  5. Traumatic elbow effusion with possible occult fracture
Answer and explanation

Traumatic elbow effusion with possible occult fracture

A visible posterior fat pad after trauma suggests an effusion and should prompt consideration of an occult intra-articular fracture.

Option explanations

Traumatic elbow effusion with possible occult fracture: A visible posterior fat pad after trauma suggests an effusion and should prompt consideration of an occult intra-articular fracture.

Radial head dislocation: A radiocapitellar line that fails to intersect the capitellum on adequate views raises concern for radial head malalignment. This is not the pattern specified in this case.

Extension-type supracondylar humerus fracture: Posterior displacement of the distal humeral fragment can place the capitellum behind the anterior humeral line. This is not the pattern specified in this case.

Normal radiographic elbow alignment: Normal radiocapitellar alignment and appropriate anterior humeral-line intersection support normal alignment but do not exclude every injury. This is not the pattern specified in this case.

Olecranon fracture: A fracture through the posterior proximal ulna at the triceps insertion identifies an olecranon injury. This is not the pattern specified in this case.
